author: joepie91_
cardQuote: I wonder whether Facebook realizes just how much damage they are going to be doing to the JS ecosystem with this approach.
quote:
Well, this is a problematic case of "throwing out the baby with the bathwater". Semantic versioning isn't the problem here (the lack of deterministic install trees is!), yet it's thrown out pretty much entirely, without even so much as considering why it exists in the first place.

I wonder whether Facebook realizes just how much damage they are going to be doing to the JS ecosystem with this approach.
storyTitle: Yarn – A new package manager for JavaScript
outcome: Yarn became a standard JavaScript package manager, now at Yarn 4 with ~12.7 million weekly npm downloads.
outcomeDetail: Yarn's lockfile and offline cache pushed npm to improve, and the project shipped Yarn 2 through Yarn 4. The yarn package still sees roughly 12.7 million weekly downloads, and Yarn is standard in many monorepos.
note: The critic feared Yarn would wreck semver and fragment the ecosystem. Deterministic lockfiles became the norm instead, and npm copied the idea.

author: anuila
cardQuote: Version 5 and this tool still has absolutely awful UX.
quote:
Version 5 and this tool still has absolutely awful UX.

I have no problem configuring Webpack, but it's ridiculous that:

- it needs two plugins to generate CSS files [1], when the homepage lists it as one of the supported outputs in front and center; [2]

- it needs a plugin have a non-trash output log. [3]

Parcel was supposed to fix the situation, and in many cases its UX is an order of magnitude better, but in exchange it brings a slew of unfixed bugs in the most simple projects that lightly sway from the base usage.

Maybe in 2030 the JS community will have figured something out.

1: https://webpack.js.org/guides/asset-management/#loading-css

2: https://webpack.js.org

3: https://github.com/GoogleChromeLabs/size-plugin
outcome: Webpack 5 shipped and webpack still sees ~73 million weekly npm downloads.
outcomeDetail: Webpack 5's persistent caching and Module Federation kept it underneath Next.js, Create React App, and many enterprise build pipelines. It remains one of the most downloaded build tools on npm.
note: The complaint about CSS plugins and output logs was fair, but it did not stop Webpack from remaining the default bundler for years. The predicted 2030 reckoning has not arrived.

author: STRiDEX
cardQuote: I'm not sure what the other use cases are since it doesn't do any of the typechecking tsc does.
quote:
Most of my projects now use babel indirectly and its been removed from all backend projects at work, sometimes replaced with typescript or vanilla es6.

Ex: anyone using facebook's jest, vue-cli, etc will get v7 whenever those packages upgrade.

The typescript support seems interesting for people with large babel pipelines, but I'm not sure what the other use cases are since it doesn't do any of the typechecking tsc does. Would be interested in hearing what people plan to use it for.

https://blogs.msdn.microsoft.com/typescript/2018/08/27/types...
outcome: @babel/core now sees ~255 million weekly npm downloads, making Babel the most-used JavaScript compiler.
outcomeDetail: Babel 7 became the standard way to compile JSX, TypeScript, and modern syntax for browsers and Node. Even projects that use TypeScript often run Babel afterward, and Babel's parser underpins much of the JS toolchain.
note: The comment read Babel's backend retreat as a loss of purpose. Babel's real moat was JSX and ecosystem plugins, which kept it at the center of front-end builds.

author: antirez
cardQuote: Spaces are the rhythm of the code... not sure why one would write code without rhythm and later add a synthetic one.
quote: I'll never understand code formatters. For me the idea of my code passing through a formatter, is like if accidentally I lost part of it: there is a lot of care in the way you write your code, even in the part that the compiler does not care about: spaces. Spaces are the rhythm of the code... not sure why one would write code without rhythm and later add a synthetic one.
outcome: Prettier became the default JavaScript formatter, used by 83% of State of JS 2021 respondents and ~180 million weekly npm downloads.
outcomeDetail: Prettier's opinionated formatting spread through editor integrations and CI checks. Its style is now the baseline for most JavaScript and TypeScript projects, and even linters adopted its formatting rules.
note: Antirez’s artisan view of spacing lost to the team-scale argument: one canonical format ends bikeshedding. Prettier made formatting a tool concern rather than a personal one.

author: Lazare
cardQuote: I was an early adopter and I got burned hard, having to rewrite everything in Mocha.
quote:
When jest was first released, it was incredibly, glacially slow, buggy, poorly documented, and seemed to be largely unmaintained. Critical features were broken and stayed broken for months. I was an early adopter and I got burned hard, having to rewrite everything in Mocha.

Since then, apparently, it has changed hugely, and is now fast, reliable, and pleasant to use. Or so I've heard; I have no particular reason to change back to jest, since mocha is fine.

But if you're wondering why you've heard about it being slow, it's because for many, many months jest was absurdly, unbelievably slow; simple "hello world" tests would take seconds, and even a medium projects would take minutes. And there was no watch mode, nor any ability to re-run failing tests, or re-run tests on changed files. It was absurd.

Edit: See, eg, https://github.com/facebook/jest/issues/116 opened 8 Aug 2014, and finally closed 17 Feb 2016. Quite a run.

Also, there were tons of bugs with the mocking and, especially, the `dontMock()` methods; many things could cause attempts to turn mocking off to silently, invisibly fail (or even more fun, to cause an attempt to disable mocking on one item to cause it to be silently, invisibly disabled on all items). It's amazingly hard to track down a failing test when a bug triggered by code in another test can cause items that should be mocked to not be mocked, and visa versa.
outcome: Jest became the most widely used JavaScript test runner, with ~60 million weekly npm downloads and a 2022 move to the OpenJS Foundation.
outcomeDetail: Jest's snapshot testing, built-in mocking, and zero-config setup made it the default in Create React App and many React projects. Meta transferred the project to the OpenJS Foundation in May 2022.
note: The comment was a scar report from Jest's early years, not a forecast. Jest's snapshot testing and speed improvements made it the default, and Mocha became the niche choice.

author: offtop5
cardQuote: Will instantly fail if you need to nav to a different domain at any point in your test.
quote:
Will instantly fail if you need to nav to a different domain at any point in your test .

Say you have happysite.com , but your using parentsite.com to authenticate, Cypress will explode instantly. If your test will ever leave your first domain, same thing.

Don't take shortcuts, use Puppeteer or it's successor Playwright
storyTitle: Cypress: Fast, easy, and reliable testing for anything that runs in a browser
outcome: Cypress added cross-origin testing with cy.origin() and still sees ~7 million weekly npm downloads.
outcomeDetail: Cypress introduced cy.origin() to handle authentication and multi-domain flows, addressing the exact limitation the comment described. It remains one of the most-used browser testing frameworks, though Playwright later overtook it.
note: The limitation was real in 2020, but Cypress shipped a workaround rather than dying. The prediction that tests would 'instantly fail' became outdated.

author: reidjs
cardQuote: We still use it, because management doesn't like the idea of how much time we've already sunk into it. Storybook is a nightmare to maintain and train devs on.
quote:
Thank you! My team was looking for a tool like this and storybook was the only one I knew about. I linked to it in slack as an option and the people delegated to implementing the component library hopped on board. After looking at how complex it was I knew it would be a terrible idea for what we needed: something very basic. I tried to veer them away from it. I even rolled my own component showcase like you were talking about before they put storybook in. No luck, they implemented storybook and after a couple months the people delegated to roll it out lost interest in it.

We still use it, because management doesn’t like the idea of how much time we’ve already sunk into it. Storybook is a nightmare to maintain and train devs on.
storyTitle: Storybook: UI component explorer for front end developers
outcome: Storybook 8 shipped in 2024 and @storybook/react still sees ~32 million weekly npm downloads.
outcomeDetail: Storybook became the industry-standard component workshop, used by thousands of teams and integrated with every major JS framework. Version 8 added visual testing and dropped React as a dependency for non-React projects.
note: The complaint about maintenance cost was real, but it described a bad rollout, not the product's trajectory. Storybook's ecosystem and framework support kept it dominant.

storyTitle: GitHub launches Actions, its workflow automation tool
outcome: GitHub Actions became GitHub's built-in CI/CD and one of the most widely used CI services.
outcomeDetail: GitHub added CI/CD to Actions in August 2019 and made it free for public repositories. Actions is now the default automation layer for millions of GitHub projects, with a large marketplace of reusable actions.
note: The snark targeted the launch's visual workflow builder, which GitHub later replaced with YAML. The underlying idea, automation attached directly to repo events, won.

author: danielsamuels
cardQuote: we tried switching over to it for a test project and it was basically a disaster
quote: Oh no, we tried switching over to it for a test project and it was basically a disaster. Something as simple as running Python tests and node tests on the same instance just didn't seem to be possible. We _really_ don't want to have to maintain our own Docker images. Their support forums are running Discourse too, so it's basically impossible to find anything you're looking for.
storyTitle: Launching Today: CircleCI 2.0 Reaches General Availability
outcome: CircleCI 2.0 became the company's core platform, and CircleCI raised $100M at a $1.7B valuation in 2021.
outcomeDetail: CircleCI 2.0's Docker-based configuration replaced the older 1.0 model and became standard for the company. By 2021 CircleCI had raised $315 million and was valued at $1.7 billion, with customers including Facebook, Coinbase, and Spotify.
note: The migration pain was real, but it was an early-adopter problem, not a product failure. CircleCI’s Docker model became the baseline for hosted CI.

author: mbrumlow
cardQuote: And with that I declare this product dead... Idera is the last stop to squeeze cash out of a company.
quote:
And with that I declare this product dead... Idera is the last stop to squeeze cash out of a company.

Expect layoffs and all future work to be outsourced via fixed cost development to lowest bidders (mostly in India ). Also expect a big sales push for multi year contracts.

Nothing wrong with India, just that companies like Idea don't like to have developers on payroll, and the ones that do write specs all day long.
outcome: Idera laid off senior Travis engineers weeks later, ended free open-source builds in 2020, and Travis suffered repeated security incidents — but the service still operates.
outcomeDetail: Within a month of the acquisition, Travis CI laid off senior engineering staff. In late 2020 it stopped providing free CI minutes for open-source projects, prompting a migration to GitHub Actions and CircleCI; later incidents exposed secrets in public repositories.
note: The comment called the private-equity playbook almost line by line: layoffs, outsourcing, and a push for multi-year contracts. Travis never recovered its position as the default CI for open source, but the product never actually died.

author: nojvek
cardQuote: Having the browser make one request per npm bundle sounds awful.
quote:
Having the browser make one request per npm bundle sounds awful. It’s great if client has fast internet and server is close by, or mostly localhost, but latency will play a far bigger role than the 50ms startup time. That’s not a good metric to look at.

The metric that corresponds to user experience is cold compile + page reload time, incremental compile + page reload time i.e. How long before I press enter on a command and I see something usable in a browser to devloop on.

If you let the browser load the first file, parse and figure out the next file to load, a large project could have 100s of roundtrips. That’s why JS bundlers were created in first place. To avoid the cost of a long critical chain.

Using a device from Africa (Uganda) to connect to US servers, one feels how bad an experience latency can make. More and more development is done on cloud machines or remote host, so this isn’t a rare usecase.

What I do hope for is if there is a new bundler, it can use the webpack plugin ecosystem. It’s massive and anything new has to foster a similar ecosystem of tooling.

Or please just make webpack fast with incremental disk compiles. I would pay money for that.
outcome: Snowpack was abandoned in April 2022; its creator moved to Astro, and Vite took the unbundled dev-server model mainstream.
outcomeDetail: Snowpack's official site now says it is no longer actively maintained and is not recommended for new projects. Vite, which combined a fast ESM dev server with a production bundler, became the default for new front-end projects.
note: The critic correctly saw that per-module requests and latency would limit the approach. Snowpack's own production story remained dependent on bundlers, and Vite executed the idea more completely.

author: meitham
cardQuote: OP suggests that having a large company behind a software tool (Microsoft in full control of Playright) is a positive thing and is an advantage over Selenium. I tend to see that negatively.
quote:
OP suggests that having a large company behind a software tool (Microsoft in full control of Playright) is a positive thing and is an advantage over Selenium.

I tend to see that negatively. Community driven projects (or non profit organisation behind them) like Python, Postgres, Firefox always are more trustworthy and likely to last longer in general.
storyTitle: Web automation: Don't use Selenium, use Playwright
outcome: Playwright became the most-used browser automation framework, with ~126 million weekly npm downloads.
outcomeDetail: Microsoft's backing let Playwright ship cross-browser support, auto-waiting, and tracing at a pace Selenium could not match. By 2026 @playwright/test saw roughly 126 million weekly downloads, far ahead of Cypress and Selenium.
note: The comment treated corporate ownership as a longevity risk. Microsoft's investment instead made Playwright the default choice for new end-to-end test suites.

author: yladiz
cardQuote: I feel like a lot of tools written like this (Vite, Vitest) are written for Vue specifically, and while of course there are reasons for building new tools that are more Vue focused, it feels like a lot of them are built partly because of not-invented-here.
quote: I'm curious what others think about this: I feel like a lot of tools written like this (Vite, Vitest) are written for Vue specifically, and while of course there are reasons for building new tools that are more Vue focused, it feels like a lot of them are built partly because of not-invented-here. I haven't been on top of the ecosystem changes so much lately, so I might be off base, but do others feel like this too? Am I missing something?
storyTitle: Vitest, fast unit-test framework powered by Vite
outcome: Vitest became the default test runner for Vite projects and now sees ~180 million weekly npm downloads.
outcomeDetail: Vitest reused Vite's transform pipeline, making it fast and configuration-light for Vue, React, Svelte, and other frameworks. It is now the recommended test runner in the Vite ecosystem and in many new framework templates.
note: The 'written for Vue' framing missed that Vite's plugin architecture was framework-agnostic. Vitest's Jest-compatible API helped it spread well beyond Vue.

author: JepZ
cardQuote: I think there is a much higher chance that it will be rendered obsolete in the near future.
quote:
Browserify, Webpack, Gulp, Grunt: everything nice and shiny, but the one JS lib that stands out for me is Rollup.js[1]

Why? Because Rollup.js makes it possible to structure code into modules in a way that is backwards compatible and future proof. Yeah it takes some getting used to and it is not yet as simple as it could be, because integrating libs which are not yet available in the module format, takes some manual configuration, but once you know how to use it you won't want to got back.

I can highly recommend it, not because it is the hottest tool out there, but because I think it has a much higher long-term value than most JS libs.

Parcel seems to have a similar functionality but due to the wide range of other functions it comes with, I think there is a much higher chance that it will be rendered obsolete in the near future. Rollup.js on the other hand _focuses_ on the combination of modules to a single bundle which will continue to be required for the foreseeable future.

[1] https://rollupjs.org
storyTitle: Parcel – A fast, zero configuration web application bundler
outcome: Parcel 2 shipped in 2021 and was used in production at Adobe, Atlassian, and Microsoft.
outcomeDetail: Parcel 2 was a ground-up rewrite with a plugin system, Rust compiler, and automatic code splitting. Adobe, Atlassian, and Microsoft used it in production, and the project remains maintained, though Vite later became the default for new projects.
note: The prediction of near-term obsolescence was wrong: Parcel survived and shipped a major rewrite. It lost the default-bundler race, but not in the way the comment expected.

author: bartvanH
cardQuote: i'm afraid gitlab is getting bloated. Why not keep the core product as a seperate thing from things like CI?
quote:
I really like the core of gitlab. It's a really good git hosting system that is easy to maintain and work with. My self hosted instance has broken only twice in the last 1.5 years and it was always because of an upgrade and it was always easily fixed.

But now i have to say i'm afraid gitlab is getting bloated. Why not keep the core product as a seperate thing from things like CI? a simple plugin style system would be enough for it to not feel like bloat but feel like extra options.
storyTitle: What’s Next for Gitlab CI: Auto DevOps
outcome: GitLab CI became a core part of GitLab's platform, which IPO'd at an ~$11 billion valuation in 2021.
outcomeDetail: GitLab integrated CI/CD directly into its product and made it a selling point against GitHub. The company priced its Nasdaq IPO at $77 per share in October 2021, valuing it at about $11 billion.
note: The concern was that bundling CI would bloat GitLab. Integration instead became GitLab's differentiator, and the CEO replied in the thread defending exactly that bet.

author: clktmr
cardQuote: But why would I as a developer want this, let alone pay for it? Isn't this the "developing in a browser" nightmare everybody was joking about a few years ago?
quote:
I can see why this is interesting from a project manager's perspective. But why would I as a developer want this, let alone pay for it? Isn't this the "developing in a browser" nightmare everybody was joking about a few years ago?

Maybe this will work for developing web applications which are executed on a remote machine by design, but everything else?
outcome: GitHub moved the majority of its own engineering work to Codespaces and made it generally available in 2021.
outcomeDetail: Codespaces moved from beta to general availability in August 2021, and GitHub's engineering team adopted it for most GitHub.com development. GitHub reported cutting codespace creation time from 45 minutes to about 10 seconds with prebuilds.
note: The 'developing in a browser' objection underestimated how much of local setup was environment maintenance. Codespaces turned that maintenance into a prebuilt, disposable container.
